subject: Communication
title: The Duchenne Smile: Real vs. Fake
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Duchenne Smile: Real vs. Fake usable.

hook.text: A politician smiles at a rally. The mouth says joy, but the eyes are empty. Something feels wrong.

buildup.text: French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne discovered in 1862 that genuine smiles involve eye muscles too.

discovery.text: A Duchenne smile crinkles the corners of the eyes. A social smile only lifts the corners of the mouth.

twist.text: About 10% of people can fake a Duchenne smile voluntarily. The rest can't — their eyes betray the truth.

climax.text: Studies link genuine Duchenne smiles in yearbook photos to better life outcomes decades later.

punchline.text: The eyes don't lie. They either smile with you or they don't.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a Duchenne smile from a fake one?

details.summary: A genuine smile, called the Duchenne smile, engages both the zygomatic major muscle around the mouth and the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eyes. Fake smiles typically move only the mouth.
details.whyItMatters: Distinguishing real from fake smiles helps read social sincerity and builds trust in personal and professional relationships.
takeaways: Duchenne smiles engage muscles around both mouth and eyes
Non-Duchenne smiles often lack eye crinkles
People intuitively rate Duchenne smiles as more trustworthy

faq.question: Can people fake a Duchenne smile convincingly?
faq.answer: Some individuals can voluntarily contract the orbicularis oculi, making detection harder. However, the timing and symmetry of a genuine Duchenne smile are difficult to replicate perfectly, so close observation can still reveal differences.

faq.question: Who was Duchenne and why is the smile named after him?
faq.answer: Guillaume Duchenne de Boulogne was a 19th-century French neurologist who used electrical stimulation to map facial muscles. He demonstrated that the eye muscle contraction distinguishes sincere smiles from posed ones.
